items.heading: Not Every Stretch of Boredom
items.text: Not Every Stretch of Boredom Not Every Stretch of Boredom Not every stretch of boredom is a plateau, and treating a temporary lull as a full-blown crisis leads to decisions you did not need to make. The difference is not how you feel on your worst day, it is duration, pattern, and whether the feeling holds up even during your good weeks.

items.heading: A Skip
items.text: A skip-level meeting, a direct, structured conversation with your manager's manager, is one of the most underused tools available inside most companies, precisely because it feels like a bold move. It is not a complaint session and not an exit interview. Used well, it is a chance to get a second, more senior read on whether the blocker is your manager or the structure, and it puts your name in front of someone who has more influence over headcount decisions than your direct manager does.

items.heading: Step 1, Set Up
items.text: Step 1, Set up the meeting through the normal channel. Ask your manager first, framed as wanting broader visibility into the team's direction, not as going around them. Most managers who are not the actual problem will support this without friction.

items.heading: Step 2, Bring One Clear
items.text: Step 2, Bring one clear ask, not a list of grievances. A useful frame: "Based on what you've seen across the org, what would it take for someone in my role to move to the next level here, and is that realistically available in this team?" That question does double duty, it signals ambition and it surfaces the structural answer directly.

items.heading: Step 3, Let Them Talk
items.text: Step 3, Let them talk more than you do. The value of a skip-level is what a more senior person tells you about the bigger picture, team budget, upcoming restructuring, plans you cannot see from your seat. Listen for those signals; they answer the Layer 3 question better than any internal job board.

items.heading: Step 4, Follow Up
items.text: Step 4, Follow up in writing within a few days. A short note referencing what was discussed and any commitment made keeps it real. If a commitment was made, a stretch project, a review at the next cycle, this note is what you point back to later.
